messages.subject: broods as clusters?
parts:
Hello all,

I'm new to the list and distance sampling, but have found the information=
=20
provided here on numerous topics very useful. Although I'm no statistical=
=20
expert, I assure you that I've done my homework on this and have yet to=20=

come across this particular situation, so I'm a bit unsure of how to=20
proceed. I am dealing with birds that occur individually "most" of the=20=

time. However, occasionally, a cluster (read: brood) is detected. Ignorin=
g=20
any cluster size bias for the moment, modeling the entire population as=20=

clusters will bias the estimate high, as only 0.5 of the population would=
=20
ever occur in clusters (broods), and fewer yet as a consequence of low=20=

brood survival. That being the case, should I model density as individual=
s,=20
and manually calculate density using a correction for sex ratio? Further,=
=20
because not all females may nest, or rear broods, even fewer than half th=
e=20
individuals occur in clusters. For example, modify equation 4.13 on pg 1=
19=20
of Buckland et al. 2001 as follows:

D^ =3D [0.5n * f(0)] + [0.5n * f(0) * sbar]

I'd appreciate any thoughts you all may have. Thanks,

Dave

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: broods as clusters?
parts:
I have communicated with David individually on this subject. You'll get
the same answer whether you partition or not as long as f(0) is the same
for single and broods. If the f(0) are not the same then you have
size-bias. I sent him a simple excel spreadsheet that showed that you
can partition the average sbar into singletons and the average sbar for
non-singletons to show how the partitioning would give the same answer.
If you want that sheet to understand it further I suggest you contact David.

regards --jeff
